entries.clue: Where you might shop for Dexter’s new diverting books (6,6)

indicatorNotes.new: A new arrangement of the same letters is still the same letters, which is all the word is asking for.
indicatorNotes.diverting: To divert something is to send it off its own path and into another, so the shuffled letters end up running through the middle of the piece beside them.

blocks.note: the Old Testament, the crossword's standard books, and these two letters open and close what follows
ten letters reset in a new order — the little word 'for' is raw material here, not a joiner

annotation.surface: Somebody wants to know where to buy Dexter's entertaining new books.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For' reads as the word joining a definition to its wordplay and is really three letters of the fodder — leave it out and the count comes up short. Colin Dexter set Inspector Morse in Oxford, which is the trap: the city is spelt out, not remembered.
annotation.definitionFit: Where you might shop → OXFORD STREET: London's main shopping street, a mile of department stores and the first place anyone names for a day's shopping.

entries.clue: Taking a Number 13, how busy, on average? (3,4,7)

indicatorNotes.Taking: A bus taking a passenger holds them inside for the journey, so the letters here close round the piece named next instead of standing beside it.
indicatorNotes.busy: A busy street has everything in it moving at once, and letters told they are busy will not stay where they were put.

blocks.note: the figure is to be written out in full, all eight letters of it
three more letters, taken from the clue exactly as it prints them
A plus No., the everyday abbreviation for number, kept whole in the middle

annotation.surface: A passenger wonders how crowded the number 13 bus usually is.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Number' does two jobs at once: it hands over its own abbreviation and it tells you the 13 beside it is to be written out as a word. The capital N is a bus route dressed up as a proper name.
annotation.definitionFit: on average → ONE WITH ANOTHER: an old idiom meaning taking one case together with the next, so it does the work of 'on average' in a sentence.

entries.clue: When the tide goes out one might view such accommodation! (5)

annotation.definition2: When the tide goes out one might view such
annotation.definitionNote: Accommodation is a mass noun in British use — nobody says accommodations — so it covers a row of homes as readily as one.

blocks.clueFragment: When the tide goes out one might view such
blocks.note: the wet sand and mud an estuary uncovers as the sea draws back goes by this same word
the ordinary British word for a home occupying one floor of a larger building

annotation.surface: At low tide you can see what sort of housing the shoreline has to offer.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark is the setter admitting there is no machinery here, only two senses of one word. Britain's tidal estuaries — the Wash, Morecambe Bay — are miles of the stuff the first half means.
annotation.definitionFit: accommodation → FLATS: a flat is a self-contained home on one floor, where Americans say apartment; the other sense is the mud an estuary uncovers.

entries.clue: Striking Brazilian moorlands discovered on tour (7)

indicatorNotes.discovered: Split it as dis-covered and it means stripped of its covers, so the letters at each end — the ones covering the rest — come off.
indicatorNotes.on tour: A side on tour is away from home and moving from place to place, which is what the letters do here.

blocks.note: nine letters with the outermost one at each end taken off, leaving seven to work with
the covering letters, M at the front and S at the back, are the two that come away

annotation.surface: A touring party comes upon some strikingly beautiful moorland in Brazil.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' is the one worth learning: read as dis-covered it takes the outside letters off rather than finding anything. Brazil's footballers go by a single name, and 'striking' says which position this one played.
annotation.definitionFit: Striking Brazilian → RONALDO: Brazil's great No 9 of the 1990s, a striker by trade and, like most Brazilian footballers, known by one name alone.

entries.clue: See 1
Pause when performing play of disreputable author (7)

indicatorNotes.of: A piece of something is part of it and not the whole, which is the cue to read inside the words that follow rather than translate them.

blocks.note: the letters run unbroken across the gap between the two words, starting some way into the first

annotation.surface: An actor breaks off mid-scene in a play by a writer of bad reputation.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing here shouts concealment: 'of' is the only signal, doing the work of 'part of'. In the theatre the word means the whole cast frozen in position, which is the pause the definition promises.
annotation.definitionFit: Pause when performing play → TABLEAU: the moment when the actors hold still in a posed group and the action stops dead, a staple of Victorian theatre and of pantomime.

entries.clue: At times rocky, otherwise mountainous country (4,5)

indicatorNotes.rocky: A rocky road is an uneven one that throws you about, and letters given a rocky ride do not land in the order they set off in.

blocks.note: seven letters of raw material, the phrase taken exactly as it stands
'or otherwise' — the two words do the same job in a sentence, so one stands in for the other

annotation.surface: The going is rocky in places and mountainous everywhere else.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At times' reads as an adverb setting up 'rocky' and is seven of the nine letters. The country is the eastern half of the island of Timor, independent of Indonesia since 2002 and almost all of it upland.
annotation.definitionFit: mountainous country → EAST TIMOR: a small south-east Asian nation built on a steep, rugged spine of mountains running the length of its half of the island.

entries.clue: Film figure’s piano recording’s retained: 16 loses nothing (3,4,7)

indicatorNotes.retained: What is retained is kept in rather than let go, so the two letters named stay inside the word in front of them.
indicatorNotes.loses: A word that loses something hands it over and carries on without it, one letter shorter than it arrived.

blocks.note: to figure something is to think it — 'I figure we're late' — and the 's is simply 'has'
an EP is a record with more tracks than a single and fewer than an album, and it lodges after the first two letters
p is the mark for piano, played softly, in written music
the word at 16 down arrives whole and gives up its O, the round letter that stands for nothing

annotation.surface: A film figure's piano recording has been kept rather than wiped.
annotation.walkthrough: The cross-reference does real work: 16 down's answer comes in entire and then drops a letter. 'Figure' is the verb rather than the noun the surface wants, and p for piano is the pianist's own shorthand.
annotation.definitionFit: Film → THE PINK PANTHER: the 1963 Blake Edwards comedy whose cartoon cat outlived the plot and gave its name to a whole run of sequels.

entries.clue: Still preferring bishop to rook, extremely optimistically (2,4)

indicatorNotes.preferring bishop to rook: On a chessboard a bishop is B and a rook R, and preferring the one to the other puts the B exactly where the R was standing.

blocks.note: a thing that is still is at rest — six letters, one of which is about to be traded

annotation.surface: A chess player still rates the bishop above the rook, which is optimistic of them.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole trick is that 'Still' is not the adverb the sentence wants but a word meaning motionless, and chess supplies the two initials that change places.
annotation.definitionFit: extremely optimistically → AT BEST: the phrase marks the most favourable reading a thing will bear — 'at best a draw' — which is optimism at its limit.

entries.clue: Personage perhaps lying in state is unknown for now (7,2,2,4)

blocks.note: a dignitary's body on public view before the funeral: what is left of them, put there for people to file past
the everyday sense: nobody can say yet, and the matter waits on events

annotation.surface: A great man's body lies in state while some question about him stays unanswered.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is the signal that the first half is an instance and not a definition — one thing a body lying in state might be said to be doing. The hinge is 'lying', which the dead do and an open question does too.
annotation.definitionFit: is unknown for now → REMAINS TO BE SEEN: the idiom for a matter events have not yet settled; the other sense is a body put on public view.

entries.clue: Day chosen for replacement of corps in retiring company, generating some power (6-8)

indicatorNotes.for replacement of: One thing put in for another takes over its place as well as its job, so the letter named next is gone and the longer word stands where it stood.
indicatorNotes.retiring: To retire is to withdraw the way you came, so the word it describes is set down back to front.

blocks.note: dies is Latin for day, the word behind diary and dial
the company you keep is your circle, and that word is written backwards here
the chosen few are the elect, five letters moving in
C is the army's own abbreviation for corps, and it is the letter that makes way

annotation.surface: A day has been fixed for a corps to be replaced inside a company that is standing down.
annotation.walkthrough: Latin gives the day — dies, as in diary — and 'company' means a circle of friends rather than a firm. The swap happens inside that circle only after it has been turned round.
annotation.definitionFit: generating some power → DIESEL-ELECTRIC: of a locomotive or ship whose diesel engine drives a generator, and the current it makes turns the wheels.

entries.clue: See 10
Keeping in touch, poorly Enigmatist’s going to take a break (5,3)

indicatorNotes.Keeping in: To keep something in is to hold it inside and not let it out, so the piece named goes within the other letters rather than after them.
indicatorNotes.poorly: Poorly means unwell, and a word in a poorly state comes out in no fit order.

blocks.note: the five letters of 'touch' reset in a new order before anything is let inside them
the setter speaking of himself: 'I'm going to' is I'll, and the apostrophe is dropped on the way in

annotation.surface: The setter, who is bad at staying in contact, is about to take a break.
annotation.walkthrough: A Guardian setter writing himself into his own clue is standard practice, and 'Enigmatist's going to' is simply 'I'll'. That is where the pair of Ls comes from; nothing of 'keeping in touch' survives but its letters.
annotation.definitionFit: take a break → CHILL OUT: to chill out is to stop, calm down and do nothing for a while, which is what taking a break comes to.

entries.clue: Ultimately harmful combo, big effects if activated (5,4)

annotation.definition: Ultimately harmful combo, big effects if activated

indicatorNotes.Ultimately: Ultimately means in the end, and the end of a written word is the single letter it finishes on.
indicatorNotes.if activated: Something activated goes off, and what goes off does not leave its parts lying where they were.

blocks.note: the final letter of the word, the one 'ultimately' points at
eight more letters, taken from the clue as they stand

annotation.surface: A mixture that does harm in the end, with big consequences once it is set off.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word here counts twice, describing the thing and handing over its letters in the same breath. What it describes is code planted quietly in a system to go off on a date or an event.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight the clue describes the thing itself: malicious code that sits harmless in a system until some condition fires it, and then does real damage.

entries.clue: Ruin preparation of minute steak: two internationals sacked (6)

indicatorNotes.preparation of: Preparing a dish means cutting it up and putting it together another way, which is what becomes of these letters.
indicatorNotes.sacked: Sacked players are dropped from the side, so the letters that stand for them leave the raw material.

blocks.note: eleven letters of raw material before anything is dropped
I is the abbreviation for international, and at cricket an international match is a Test: both sets of letters come out

annotation.surface: A minute steak is being prepared on the day two international players are dropped.
annotation.walkthrough: Two senses of 'international' are wanted at once, the abbreviation and cricket's word for a match between countries, and both are lurking in the steak. Six letters are left, and 'preparation' shuffles them.
annotation.definitionFit: Ruin → UNMAKE: to unmake a thing is to undo the making of it, and what has been unmade is ruined as surely as if it had been smashed.

entries.clue: Cover one’s tracks maybe to achieve objective (6)

indicatorNotes.maybe: Maybe flags an example rather than a definition: this is one of the things a track gets covered with, not the word for all of them.

blocks.note: the black stuff spread over a road surface, which is one way a track gets covered
to get a result is to achieve it

annotation.surface: Someone hides the traces of where they have been in order to get what they want.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cover one's tracks' is a whole idiom in the surface, meaning to hide your traces, and the clue wants it literally instead — the stuff a track is covered with. 'To' joins the halves and adds nothing.
annotation.definitionFit: objective → TARGET: the thing being aimed at, whether a mark on a range or the figure a department has to hit by the end of the year.

entries.clue: See 1
Fire obsessive bouncer for pinching clubber’s bottom (7)

indicatorNotes.pinching: Pinching here is gripping between finger and thumb rather than stealing, so the word closes on the letter and keeps it inside.
indicatorNotes.bottom: The bottom of a word is the letter it ends on, which in a down entry is also the one sitting lowest in the grid.

blocks.note: the tiger in Winnie-the-Pooh who cannot stop bouncing, since bouncing is what Tiggers do best
the last letter of that word

annotation.surface: A doorman with a fixation is being sacked for pinching a clubber's backside.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a nightclub sacking, and 'Fire' looks like the verb doing the sacking. It is the definition instead, and the rest of the sentence turns out to be a children's book.
annotation.definitionFit: Fire → TRIGGER: to trigger something is to set it off, which is what firing a gun does, and both words take an object the same way.

entries.clue: Very good supports covering us when blasting? (8)

indicatorNotes.covering: What covers a thing hides it from view, so the two letters named next are buried in the longer word and are pulled out of it.
indicatorNotes.when blasting: A blast leaves nothing standing where it stood, and letters caught in one come down in another order.

blocks.note: pi is the crossword's word for pious — so good it is insufferable
the eight letters of the definition doing a second job, with the two spelling 'us' taken out and the remaining six rearranged
the pair of letters hiding in the longer word, and the pair that does not survive

annotation.surface: The supports shielding us while the blasting goes on are doing an excellent job.
annotation.walkthrough: One word works twice over: 'supports' is the definition and it is also the letters, minus the us it conceals. PI for pious is worth keeping — it turns up wherever a clue says holy or sanctimonious.
annotation.definitionFit: supports → PIT PROPS: the timber or steel posts that hold up the roof of a coal mine and keep the workings from coming down on the miners.

entries.clue: School’s out when psychologist waves pen (6)

indicatorNotes.School’s out: When school is out everyone in it has left, and the six letters spelling it leave the longer word.
indicatorNotes.waves: A wave runs through a thing and leaves it rippling, so the letters it passes through settle in a different order.

blocks.note: twelve letters, and the word the whole clue works on
all six of these letters are present in the longer word, and they are the ones that go

annotation.surface: A psychologist waves a pen about now that school has finished for the day.
annotation.walkthrough: A school of thought is the tempting reading, and it is really a plain deletion: the six letters of 'school' come out of the psychologist. The pen left at the end is an animal's, not a writer's.
annotation.definitionFit: pen → PIGSTY: a pen is any small enclosure for livestock, and this is the one pigs are kept in, walled and roofed at one end.

entries.clue: This bar’s swinging ex-Palace favourite who likes scoring after gin (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a whole statement rather than a noun: the answer is the swinging bar the clue is pointing at, and 'this' does the pointing.

indicatorNotes.after: In a down entry what comes after a thing sits below it, so the footballer goes underneath the snare rather than in front of it.

blocks.note: a gin is a snare for catching game, nothing to do with the drink a bar would pour
Eberechi Eze, the goalscoring midfielder who left Crystal Palace, the south London club everyone calls Palace

annotation.surface: The bar is lively tonight, with a former Palace star who likes to score among the crowd.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scoring' keeps the surface in the nightclub while pointing at goals, and the footballer's short name is the piece nobody sees coming. A gin here is the old trapper's snare.
annotation.definitionFit: This bar’s swinging → TRAPEZE: the horizontal bar hung from two ropes that a circus acrobat swings on, so the clue's sentence is literally true of it.

entries.clue: See 7
A cracking feature set into low floor in the middle of a lounge? (8,6)

annotation.definitionNote: The clue offers a noun, a spell of lounging, where the answer is the -ing form of a verb; both name the same idle activity.

indicatorNotes.cracking: A crack splits a thing open along its length, so the letter named goes into the split rather than onto either end.
indicatorNotes.set into: What is set into something is fixed inside it, the way a stone is set into a ring.
indicatorNotes.in the middle of: This says where: between the two pieces already named, not in front of them or behind.

blocks.note: the noise cattle make: cows low in the byre
a feature of a face, the one that juts out at the bottom of it
the ground is the floor you stand on out of doors, and it is the word that gets cracked open
the clue's own opening word, taken as the single letter it is

annotation.surface: An estate agent points out a cracking feature set into the low floor of a lounge.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cracking' is the estate agent's word for excellent in the surface and a physical split in the wordplay. 'Low' is the cow's noise, one of the crossword's standing tricks, and the floor meant is out of doors.
annotation.definitionFit: a lounge → MOOCHING AROUND: to mooch around is to drift about with nothing much to do, which is what a lounge about amounts to.

entries.clue: See 21
There but for all to see, our most prominent, looking skyward? (5)

annotation.definition: There but for all to see, our most prominent, looking skyward?

indicatorNotes.but: But here means except, so what follows it is the part left out rather than a part put in.
indicatorNotes.looking skyward: In a down entry the sky is at the top, so a piece told to look that way is read upwards, last letter first.

blocks.note: the clue's own word, three letters, before anything is taken out of it
a film rated U is Universal, passed for everyone to watch, and this is the letter that drops out
the most prominent of anything is No 1, written as No plus the Roman figure for one, then read the other way up

annotation.surface: The brightest thing in our night sky is plainly there for anyone who looks up.
annotation.walkthrough: Read straight, the sentence is a remark about the night sky; read again, every word of it is an instruction. The film certificate U, for Universal, is the piece that has to go.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight the whole clue describes the constellation: the most conspicuous figure in our night sky, visible to the naked eye from either hemisphere.

entries.clue: Considered Scotswoman correct to hide face away from sundown to sunrise (7,3,5)

indicatorNotes.to hide face away: A word's face is the letter it starts with, and hiding that away takes it off the front and buries it inside the word standing first.

blocks.note: what you considered, you thought: seven letters that open up to take a visitor in
hen is what a Glaswegian calls a woman, the Scots equivalent of a Londoner's love
correct is right, five letters whose first is about to go missing from the front of them

annotation.surface: Somebody thought the Scotswoman was right to keep her face hidden all night.
annotation.walkthrough: The letter that hides is the one 'correct' begins with, and it goes into another word rather than out of the clue altogether. Nothing is lost, which is why the letters still add up.
annotation.definitionFit: from sundown to sunrise → THROUGH THE NIGHT: the phrase covers the whole span of darkness without a break, which is dusk to dawn exactly.

entries.clue: Top director, top tester and theatre’s top checker (6,6)

indicatorNotes.top tester: To top a man is to behead him, which is what happens to the word for a tester: it loses the letter at its head.
indicatorNotes.theatre’s top: The top of a written word is the letter it begins with, the same word in a quite different sense.

blocks.note: a tester is a prober, one who probes, and it arrives a letter short at the front
the first letter of that word as the clue spells it
to rein a thing in is to check it, and one who does the reining takes the -er

annotation.surface: One man is the best director going, the best tester and the theatre's best inspector.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Top' turns up three times and means something different each time: best in the definition, beheaded in the middle, first letter at the end. The man himself directed This Is Spinal Tap and When Harry Met Sally.
annotation.definitionFit: Top director → ROBERT REINER: the American film-maker behind This Is Spinal Tap, Stand By Me and When Harry Met Sally, who works as Rob.
